clue.text: Demands and obtains kiss in ultimately lamentable performances

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the next word is used
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so a piece goes into the middle of the rest

blocks.note: the last letter of lamentable
X is the usual crossword kiss, as signed at the foot of a letter
acts are turns or performances on stage

explanation.surface: Someone who stages dreadful shows still insists on getting a kiss afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: The kiss X goes inside E + ACTS, giving E-X-ACTS. The definition is the whole phrase 'Demands and obtains', which is exactly what exacting a payment means.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact something is to insist on it and then actually get it, like a tax or promise extracted.

clue.text: Guess teatime's off?

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word taken letter for letter, with its S

explanation.surface: A puzzled guess about whether the afternoon tea has been cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guess' reads as a verb opening a question, but it is the definition; the possessive's S is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An estimate is an approximate judgement or rough calculation, which is what a guess amounts to.

clue.text: When computer's overwhelming Everyman's a kind of jelly

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf and swallow up, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
PC is a personal computer; the 's is 'has'
the setter Everyman refers to himself, so this is I (the 's is 'is')

explanation.surface: A setter complaining about being swamped by a computer, oddly ending in jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own name stands for I, placed inside PC, all after AS: AS + P(I)C.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury gelatine made from meat stock, used to set cold dishes.

clue.text: Cricket match on TV: fourth of batsmen in experimental gear

indicators.note: fourth of picks out the letter standing in fourth position of the following word

blocks.note: a Test is an international cricket match
the tube is informal for television
B-A-T-S: the fourth letter

explanation.surface: Watching a televised cricket match, with a batsman in odd-looking kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Experimental gear' sounds like trial cricket equipment, but it is laboratory glassware. A Test match is a full international game of cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Test tubes are the thin glass vessels used in laboratory experiments, standard scientific equipment.

clue.text: The red flag or The Stars and Stripes Forever?

blocks.note: first meaning: a flag or banner carried as an emblem
second meaning: a well-known tune everyone plays, here a famous Sousa march

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves look like songs, since The Red Flag is a socialist anthem, but the first is taken literally as a banner and the second, the march, as a classic tune.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a banner flown as an emblem and an established piece of music that performers keep returning to.

clue.text: Blockbuster, tall tale with orc, rebooted

indicators.note: a reboot restarts and reshapes a film franchise, so the letters are made over in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A film pitch: a fantasy yarn featuring an orc, remade as a big summer hit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like film talk, and 'rebooted' fits, but here it just means the letters are set going again in a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: Total Recall is a 1990 Schwarzenegger science-fiction film, a big-budget hit that was itself remade in 2012.

clue.text: Invaders laying waste to Australian navy: they're expected

indicators.note: laying waste destroys things, so certain letters are wiped out of the word

blocks.note: the Normans invaded England in 1066
A is the abbreviation for Australian
N is the abbreviation for navy

explanation.surface: Raiders wrecking an Australian fleet, and everyone saw it coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian navy' suggests RAN, but it is two separate abbreviations, A and N, both struck out of NORMANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Norms are standards of behaviour that society expects people to follow.

clue.text: See our way to resort? Don't worry

indicators.note: read as re-sort, meaning to sort again into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone reassuring a friend about finding their way to a holiday resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday destination; split as re-sort it tells you to reorder the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a command telling people to carry on and ignore an interruption, a reassurance that nothing needs attention.

clue.text: Two posters stuck up displaying avant-garde art

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up turns it to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a poster is an advertisement, AD, and two of them make AD AD

explanation.surface: A pair of posters pasted on a wall showing modern art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up' reads naturally as pasting posters on a wall; in a down answer it means reading upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Dada was an early twentieth-century anti-art movement, among the most provocative avant-garde styles.

clue.text: Toiler you picture inputting something thunderously, primarily?

definitions.text: Toiler you picture inputting something thunderously, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so the first letter of each word is taken

blocks.clueFragment: Toiler you picture inputting something thunderously
blocks.note: the opening letters of the six words

explanation.surface: Imagine a worker hammering loudly at a keyboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials spell the answer, and the whole clue also describes it: a worker you imagine bashing out text noisily on a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A typist is a worker whose job is keying text, often clattering away at a typewriter.

clue.text: Celebrated audibly in multiple flights

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so a word is replaced by one pronounced identically

blocks.note: storied means famous in stories and legend

explanation.surface: Someone cheered loudly aboard several aeroplane journeys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flights' suggests air travel; here it means flights of stairs, one per floor of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A storeyed building has several floors, each reached by its own flight of stairs.

clue.text: Victorian cuisine: scoff a kind of dove, very excited

blocks.note: to scoff at is to mock
the turtle dove
so means very, as in 'so tired'
up can mean excited or aroused, as in 'all up'

explanation.surface: A thrilled diner in the 1800s wolfing down a dove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' looks like eating greedily, which suits the menu, but it means jeer; the final SOUP is built from two small words.
explanation.definitionFit: Mock turtle soup was a popular Victorian dish imitating green turtle soup, usually made with calf's head.

clue.text: Music and cakes for guttersnipes

blocks.note: a raga is a melodic form in Indian classical music
muffins are small cakes

explanation.surface: Tunes and buns laid on as a treat for street children.
explanation.walkthrough: A raga is a traditional Indian musical form, and a guttersnipe is a scruffy child of the streets.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragamuffins are ragged, dirty children, the same idea as street urchins living rough.

clue.text: 'Athirst' regularly rejected, being archaic: that's agreed

indicators.note: throwing away letters at regular intervals leaves only the ones in between

blocks.note: discard A, H, R, T and keep the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned word turned down for being out of date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' tempts you to reverse something; here it is the odd letters that are thrown out. 'Being archaic' flags the old-fashioned form of 'it is'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tis, short for it is, is an old poetic way of confirming a statement, like saying yes, indeed.

clue.text: Charmers, ones that are often fruity

blocks.note: first meaning: suave, smooth-talking people
second meaning: blended drinks usually made from fruit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruity' can describe a suggestive charmer too, so both halves seem to describe one type of person; the second is really a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both slick, ingratiating people and thick blended drinks usually made with fresh fruit.

clue.text: Brigade, the unruly kind

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly and out of control, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A disorderly military brigade, the rowdy sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' reads as a noun, 'the unruly sort', but it is the adjective meaning generous and caring.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone big-hearted is generous and warmly sympathetic, the same as a kind person.

clue.text: Once again enthral, seeing cabbages pruned and half of fragrant sprigs

indicators.note: pruning cuts off part of a plant, so a letter is lopped from the front
keeping half means the other half of the letters is dropped

blocks.note: greens are leafy vegetables such as cabbage; lose the G
sprigs of lavender are prized for scent; keep the first four letters

explanation.surface: A gardener captivated again by trimmed cabbages and sweet-smelling herbs.
explanation.walkthrough: GREENS loses its first letter and LAVENDER keeps only its first half, giving REENS + LAVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthral originally meant to make someone a thrall or slave, so enthral once more means make a slave again.

clue.text: Chart with an old record climbing: it's Spanish

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means going upward, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old
an LP is a long-playing vinyl record
a chart is a map

explanation.surface: A song chart with a golden oldie rising up it, and it's a Spanish hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chart' and 'climbing' suggest the pop charts; MAP with AN, O and LP is written upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Pamplona is a city in northern Spain, famous for its bull-running festival.

clue.text: Endlessly devour exotic tea that's excellent

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
exotic means strange and foreign, so the letters take an unfamiliar arrangement

blocks.note: to devour is to consume; lose its last letter
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Gulp down a strange foreign brew, which turns out to be delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: CONSUME drops its E to CONSUM, then TEA is rearranged to MATE, which is also a South American tea, a nice touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Consummate as an adjective means supremely skilled or perfect, a stronger synonym of excellent.

clue.text: English getting runs? One, for a long stretch

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs
A means one, as in 'a pound'

explanation.surface: An English batsman scoring runs, one who stays in for a long innings.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of a long stay at the crease is a cover; 'a long stretch' means a span of history.
explanation.definitionFit: An era is a lengthy period of history marked by some shared character.

clue.text: Out of Sellotape now, all of a sudden

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or not in place, so the letters are knocked into new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; Sellotape is the British brand name for clear sticky tape

explanation.surface: Someone suddenly discovering the sticky tape has run out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of' reads as a single phrase meaning 'having none'; only 'Out' signals the rearrangement and 'of' joins the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom, from Macbeth, means everything happening in a single sudden action rather than gradually.

clue.text: A plan's arranged, not initially paying through the nose

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so just the opening letter of the word is meant
not means without, so that letter is removed
arranging puts things in a fresh order, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, with the S
the first letter of paying

explanation.surface: A scheme drawn up to avoid paying over the odds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paying through the nose' is an idiom for being overcharged, but the first word goes to the wordplay and 'through the nose' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasal describes sound produced with air passing out by way of the nostrils, as in a nasal voice.

clue.text: Swears, finding piece of haggis in porridge earlier

definitions.note: a plural noun here, as in 'swears and curses'

indicators.note: a piece is a small part, here the single opening letter
one thing put in another sits inside it, splitting the outer word

blocks.note: before it is cooked, porridge is oats
the first letter of haggis

explanation.surface: A Scot cursing on finding a lump of haggis in the morning porridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swears' looks like a verb but is a plural noun here. Haggis is a Scottish dish of offal, and porridge is made from oats.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaths are curses or profanities, informally called swears or swear words.

clue.text: To some extent get along with other people

indicators.note: to some extent means partly, so only a portion of the following words is used

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Someone who manages, more or less, to get on with others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get along with other people' reads as one phrase about sociability; the definition begins at 'with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al. is Latin shorthand for 'and others', used after a first name in lists of authors.

clue.text: Alpinist's regrettable lack of control

indicators.note: something regrettable has gone wrong, so the letters are in a sorry mess

blocks.note: taken as written; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A climber's unfortunate slip, losing their grip on the mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's stands for 'is', joining the fodder to its indicator; 'regrettable' tells you the climber's name is scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailspin is a spiralling dive by an aircraft, and figuratively any state of chaotic collapse or panic.

clue.text: Socialist in Caracas: Trotskyist?

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the start of the next

explanation.surface: Asking whether a left-winger in Venezuela's capital follows Trotsky.
explanation.walkthrough: Caracas is the capital of Venezuela; the Latin American setting fits the Cuban revolutionary.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro led Cuba's communist revolution and ruled as a socialist head of state for decades.

clue.text: An absent-minded shopper might be this vacant

definitions.text: An absent-minded shopper might be this

blocks.clueFragment: An absent-minded shopper might be this
blocks.note: first meaning, read playfully: without a shopping list
second meaning: blank, lacking energy or interest

explanation.walkthrough: The first half splits the word into its parts, a shopper who forgot the list; the second is the ordinary meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The ordinary sense is languid and lacking energy or enthusiasm, like a vacant expression or mood.

clue.text: Read third letter aloud depicting Biblical impediment

indicators.note: aloud means spoken, so the words are replaced by others that are pronounced the same

blocks.note: read in the past tense is said like the colour, and C is the third letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: Instructions to say a letter out loud, as a child learning to read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read' is the past tense, sounding like the colour, not the present tense.
explanation.definitionFit: In Exodus the Red Sea blocked the Israelites' escape from Egypt until Moses parted its waters.
